concepts.title: The Earth - Shape, Structure, and Atmosphere
concepts.definition: The Earth is an oblate spheroid planet with layers (crust, mantle, core) and an atmosphere of gases that supports life.
concepts.key_idea: The Earth is round, has a layered structure, and is surrounded by an atmosphere that makes life possible.
question_patterns: What is the shape of the Earth?
Name the main layers of the Earth.
What is the atmosphere and why is it important?
Why is the Earth called a unique planet?
Which gases make up the Earth's atmosphere?

solution_steps.explain: State that the Earth is round, slightly flattened at the poles, called an oblate spheroid.
Name the crust, mantle, and core as the three main layers of the Earth.
Describe the blanket of gases (nitrogen, oxygen, etc.) that surrounds the Earth and supports life.

worked_examples.question: What is the shape of the Earth?
worked_examples.solution: The Earth is round but slightly flattened at the poles, which is called an oblate spheroid.
worked_examples.answer: An oblate spheroid, slightly flattened at the poles.

worked_examples.question: Name the main layers of the Earth.
worked_examples.solution: The three main layers are the crust, the mantle, and the core.
worked_examples.answer: Crust, mantle, and core.

worked_examples.question: Why is the Earth called a unique planet?
worked_examples.solution: The Earth is unique because it has water, a life-supporting atmosphere, and suitable temperatures for living things.
worked_examples.answer: It has water, a life-supporting atmosphere, and right temperatures.

exercises.question: What is the atmosphere and why is it important?
Which gases make up the Earth's atmosphere?
Give one reason why the Earth supports life.

concepts.title: Rotation and Revolution of the Earth
concepts.definition: Rotation is the spinning of the Earth on its axis, and revolution is the movement of the Earth around the Sun in an orbit.
concepts.formula: rotation period = 24 hours; revolution period = 365.25 days
concepts.key_idea: The Earth spins on its axis (rotation) causing day and night, and moves around the Sun (revolution) causing a year.
question_patterns: What is the difference between rotation and revolution of the Earth?
How long does the Earth take to complete one rotation?
How long does the Earth take to complete one revolution?
What causes day and night on Earth?
What is the axis of the Earth?

solution_steps.explain: Determine whether the question is about spinning on the axis (rotation) or orbiting the Sun (revolution).
Use the known period: rotation takes 24 hours and revolution takes 365.25 days.
Give the time taken for the identified motion.

worked_examples.question: How long does the Earth take to complete one rotation?
worked_examples.solution: The Earth takes about 24 hours to complete one rotation on its axis.
worked_examples.answer: 24 hours.

worked_examples.question: How long does the Earth take to complete one revolution?
worked_examples.solution: The Earth takes about 365.25 days to complete one revolution around the Sun.

worked_examples.question: What is the difference between rotation and revolution of the Earth?
worked_examples.solution: Rotation is the Earth spinning on its axis, while revolution is the Earth moving around the Sun in an orbit.
worked_examples.answer: Rotation is spinning on the axis; revolution is orbiting the Sun.

exercises.question: What causes day and night on Earth?
What is the axis of the Earth?
How many rotations does the Earth make in one year approximately?

concepts.title: Day and Night Cycle
concepts.definition: The day and night cycle occurs because the Earth rotates on its axis, causing one half to face the Sun (day) while the other half faces away (night).
concepts.key_idea: Day and night are caused by the rotation of the Earth; the side facing the Sun has day and the opposite side has night.
question_patterns: What causes day and night on the Earth?
Why does the Sun appear to rise in the east?
How long is one day on the Earth?
Why do different places have different times of day?
Explain the day and night cycle with a diagram.

solution_steps.explain: Note that the Earth spins on its axis from west to east.
The half of the Earth facing the Sun has day, and the half facing away has night.
As the Earth rotates, each place moves into and out of sunlight, creating the day and night cycle.

worked_examples.question: What causes day and night on the Earth?
worked_examples.solution: Day and night are caused by the rotation of the Earth on its axis.
worked_examples.answer: The rotation of the Earth on its axis.

worked_examples.question: Why does the Sun appear to rise in the east?
worked_examples.solution: Because the Earth rotates from west to east, the Sun appears to rise in the east and set in the west.
worked_examples.answer: The Earth rotates west to east, so the Sun appears to rise in the east.

worked_examples.question: How long is one day on the Earth?
worked_examples.solution: One day on the Earth is about 24 hours, which is the time for one rotation.
worked_examples.answer: 24 hours.

exercises.question: Why do different places have different times of day?
Explain the day and night cycle with a diagram.
Why does the Sun appear to move across the sky?

concepts.title: Seasons and Their Causes
concepts.definition: Seasons are caused by the tilt of the Earth's axis and its revolution around the Sun, which changes the amount of sunlight different parts of the Earth receive.
concepts.key_idea: The tilt of the Earth's axis combined with its revolution causes seasons by changing how directly sunlight falls on different regions.
question_patterns: What causes the seasons on the Earth?
Why is it summer in one hemisphere and winter in the other at the same time?
How does the tilt of the Earth's axis affect seasons?
Name the four seasons in order.
Why do places near the equator not have distinct seasons?

solution_steps.explain: Note that the Earth's axis is tilted at about 23.5 degrees from the vertical.
As the Earth revolves, the tilt causes one hemisphere to receive more direct sunlight than the other.
The hemisphere tilted towards the Sun has summer, and the one tilted away has winter.

worked_examples.question: What causes the seasons on the Earth?
worked_examples.solution: Seasons are caused by the tilt of the Earth's axis and its revolution around the Sun, which changes how much sunlight each part receives.
worked_examples.answer: The tilt of the axis and revolution around the Sun.

worked_examples.question: Why is it summer in one hemisphere and winter in the other at the same time?
worked_examples.solution: Because the axis is tilted, one hemisphere leans towards the Sun (summer) while the other leans away (winter).
worked_examples.answer: One hemisphere tilts towards the Sun and the other away.

worked_examples.question: Name the four seasons in order.
worked_examples.solution: The four seasons in order are summer, autumn, winter, and spring.
worked_examples.answer: Summer, autumn, winter, spring.

exercises.question: How does the tilt of the Earth's axis affect seasons?
Why do places near the equator not have distinct seasons?
Give one example of how seasons affect daily life.

concepts.title: The Moon - Phases and Surface
concepts.definition: The Moon is the Earth's natural satellite; its phases change as its position relative to the Earth and Sun changes, and its surface has craters, mountains, and plains.
concepts.key_idea: The Moon shows different phases because we see different portions of its sunlit side as it orbits the Earth.
question_patterns: What are the phases of the Moon?
Why does the Moon change its shape?
What is the surface of the Moon like?
Why does the Moon shine?
How long does the Moon take to orbit the Earth?

solution_steps.explain: Note where the Moon is in its orbit around the Earth relative to the Sun.
Find how much of the Moon's sunlit side is visible from the Earth.
Identify the phase (new moon, crescent, half, gibbous, or full moon) based on the visible portion.

worked_examples.question: What are the phases of the Moon?
worked_examples.solution: The main phases are new moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full moon, waning gibbous, last quarter, and waning crescent.
worked_examples.answer: New moon, crescent, quarter, gibbous, and full moon.

worked_examples.question: Why does the Moon change its shape?
worked_examples.solution: The Moon's shape appears to change because we see different portions of its sunlit side as it orbits the Earth.
worked_examples.answer: We see different portions of the sunlit side as the Moon orbits the Earth.

worked_examples.question: Why does the Moon shine?
worked_examples.solution: The Moon shines because it reflects sunlight falling on its surface; it does not produce its own light.
worked_examples.answer: The Moon reflects sunlight.

exercises.question: What is the surface of the Moon like?
How long does the Moon take to orbit the Earth?
Why do we see only one side of the Moon from the Earth?

concepts.title: Eclipses - Solar and Lunar
concepts.definition: A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon comes between the Sun and the Earth, blocking sunlight; a lunar eclipse occurs when the Earth comes between the Sun and the Moon, casting a shadow on the Moon.
concepts.key_idea: Eclipses happen when the Sun, Moon, and Earth align so that one body blocks light from reaching another.
question_patterns: What is a solar eclipse?
What is a lunar eclipse?
What is the difference between a solar and a lunar eclipse?
Why do eclipses not occur every month?
Why should we not look at a solar eclipse with naked eyes?

solution_steps.explain: Check which body is between the other two: Moon between Sun and Earth, or Earth between Sun and Moon.
See which body is in shadow: the Earth during a solar eclipse, or the Moon during a lunar eclipse.
If the Moon blocks the Sun it is a solar eclipse; if the Earth blocks sunlight from the Moon it is a lunar eclipse.

worked_examples.question: What is a solar eclipse?
worked_examples.solution: A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon comes between the Sun and the Earth and blocks the Sun's light from reaching the Earth.
worked_examples.answer: The Moon blocks the Sun's light from reaching the Earth.

worked_examples.question: What is a lunar eclipse?
worked_examples.solution: A lunar eclipse occurs when the Earth comes between the Sun and the Moon and casts its shadow on the Moon.
worked_examples.answer: The Earth casts a shadow on the Moon.

worked_examples.question: Why do eclipses not occur every month?
worked_examples.solution: Eclipses do not occur every month because the Moon's orbit is tilted relative to the Earth's orbit around the Sun, so alignment is rare.
worked_examples.answer: The Moon's orbit is tilted, so perfect alignment is rare.

exercises.question: What is the difference between a solar and a lunar eclipse?
Why should we not look at a solar eclipse with naked eyes?
Draw a diagram showing a lunar eclipse.

concepts.title: The Sun and Sunlight
concepts.definition: The Sun is a star at the centre of the solar system made of hot gases; it provides light and heat energy that sustains life on Earth.
concepts.key_idea: The Sun is a huge ball of hot gases that provides the energy needed for life and drives weather and seasons on Earth.
question_patterns: What is the Sun made of?
Why is the Sun important for life on Earth?
What is the structure of the Sun?
How does the Sun produce energy?
Give one effect of the Sun on the Earth.

solution_steps.explain: State that the Sun is a star made of hot gases, mainly hydrogen and helium.
Mention the main parts such as the core, photosphere, and corona.
Explain that the Sun provides light and heat that support life, weather, and the water cycle on Earth.

worked_examples.question: What is the Sun made of?
worked_examples.solution: The Sun is made of hot gases, mainly hydrogen and helium.
worked_examples.answer: Hot gases, mainly hydrogen and helium.

worked_examples.question: Why is the Sun important for life on Earth?
worked_examples.solution: The Sun provides light and heat energy needed for plants to make food, for warmth, and for the water cycle, all of which support life.
worked_examples.answer: It provides light and heat energy that support life.

worked_examples.question: Give one effect of the Sun on the Earth.
worked_examples.solution: The Sun's heat causes water to evaporate, which drives the water cycle and weather.
worked_examples.answer: It drives the water cycle and weather.

exercises.question: What is the structure of the Sun?
How does the Sun produce energy?
Give one reason why the Sun is called a star.

concepts.title: Stars and Constellations
concepts.definition: Stars are huge balls of hot glowing gases that produce their own light; a constellation is a group of stars that forms a recognisable pattern in the night sky.
concepts.key_idea: Stars make their own light and appear small because they are very far away; constellations are patterns formed by groups of stars.
question_patterns: What is a star?
Why do stars appear so small?
What is a constellation?
Name one well-known constellation.
Why do stars twinkle?

solution_steps.explain: State that a star is a huge ball of hot gases that produces its own light.
Note that stars appear small because they are very far away from the Earth.
Explain that a constellation is a recognised pattern formed by a group of stars in the sky.

worked_examples.question: What is a star?
worked_examples.solution: A star is a huge ball of hot glowing gases that produces its own light and heat.
worked_examples.answer: A huge ball of hot gases that makes its own light.

worked_examples.question: Why do stars appear so small?
worked_examples.solution: Stars appear small because they are very, very far away from the Earth.
worked_examples.answer: Because they are very far away.

worked_examples.question: Name one well-known constellation.
worked_examples.solution: The Big Dipper (Saptarshi in India) is a well-known constellation shaped like a ladle.
worked_examples.answer: The Big Dipper (Saptarshi).

exercises.question: What is a constellation?

concepts.title: Solar System Overview
concepts.definition: The solar system consists of the Sun at the centre and eight planets, along with their moons, asteroids, and comets, that orbit the Sun.
concepts.key_idea: The solar system has the Sun at its centre and eight planets that revolve around it in fixed paths called orbits.
question_patterns: What is the solar system?
Name the eight planets of the solar system in order.
Which planet is closest to the Sun?
What is an orbit?
Name one dwarf planet in the solar system.

solution_steps.explain: Note that the Sun is at the centre of the solar system.
Recall that there are eight planets that orbit the Sun.
Name the planets from the Sun outward: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.

worked_examples.question: Name the eight planets of the solar system in order.
worked_examples.solution: The eight planets in order from the Sun are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune.
worked_examples.answer: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.

worked_examples.question: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
worked_examples.solution: Mercury is the planet closest to the Sun.
worked_examples.answer: Mercury.

worked_examples.question: What is the solar system?
worked_examples.solution: The solar system is the Sun and all the objects that orbit it, including the eight planets, their moons, asteroids, and comets.
worked_examples.answer: The Sun and everything that orbits it.
